q: Why is binary search O(log n)?
a1: Every step looks at the middle element and throws away half of the array. Halving n until 1 item is left takes about log2(n) steps.
a2: Because each comparison halves the remaining search space, so for n items you need roughly log n comparisons, e.g. about 20 for a million items.

q: What is a base case in recursion?
a1: It is the condition where the function stops calling itself and returns directly, like n == 0 for factorial.
a2: The base case is the simplest input that is answered without recursion. Without it the calls never stop and Python raises RecursionError.

q: Why does my DFS on a grid never finish?
a1: You are probably not marking cells as visited, so DFS keeps going back to cells it has already seen. Keep a visited set.
a2: DFS revisits cells forever if you never record which ones you've explored. Add each cell to a visited set before exploring its neighbours.

q: Why is building a heap with heapify O(n)?
a1: Most nodes are near the bottom and only move down a little, so the total work adds up to about 2n, not n log n.
a2: heapify sifts down from the last parent to the root; nodes low in the tree have short paths, so the sum over all nodes is linear.

q: When should I use dynamic programming?
a1: When the same subproblems repeat, like in fibonacci or coin change. Store their answers so each is solved only once.
a2: Use DP if a recursive solution keeps solving identical subproblems; memoize or build a table bottom-up to avoid the repeated work.
